title: Sushi for a Hangover: Is It Good? What to Order and What to Skip
excerpt: Is sushi good for a hangover? How rice, miso soup, salt, and ginger help, whether raw fish is okay the morning after, the best order, and the soy sauce trap.
metaDescription: Is sushi good for a hangover? How rice, miso soup, and ginger help, whether raw fish is okay, the best order, and why to go easy on soy sauce.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** sushi is a pretty good hangover meal, mostly for boring reasons. The rice gives you easy carbohydrates when your blood sugar may be low, the miso soup that usually comes with it brings salt and warm fluid, and the pickled ginger can help settle a queasy stomach. It won't cure a hangover, and nothing on the menu "detoxes" your liver. But if sushi sounds good to you the morning after, there's no reason to talk yourself out of it, as long as you order sensibly and go easy on the soy sauce.

**The quick version of what to order:** a bowl of miso soup, a few simple rolls or nigiri built around rice and cooked or very fresh fish, some edamame, pickled ginger on the side, and plenty of water or unsweetened green tea. Skip the tempura-and-spicy-mayo rolls if your stomach is shaky, keep soy sauce to a light dip, and don't order a beer or sake "to take the edge off."

> **When a hangover is more than a hangover.** Food helps an ordinary rough morning. It doesn't fix a medical problem. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for many hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or worsening belly pain, you're confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, or you have a racing heart, chest pain, or trouble breathing. If someone is unresponsive, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has blue-tinged lips after drinking, that can be alcohol poisoning: call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away. And if you notice shaking, sweating, or anxiety that starts when you stop drinking after several days of heavy use, talk to a doctor, because that can be early withdrawal rather than a hangover.

## Why Sushi Works for a Hangover: The Short Science

A hangover isn't one thing. Researchers who study it describe a mix of overlapping problems: dehydration and lost salts, an upset stomach, low blood sugar, poor sleep, inflammation, and the after-effects of your body breaking down alcohol. No single food addresses all of that. What a good hangover meal can do is take the pressure off a few of those problems at once, and sushi happens to hit several of them.

### 1. The rice: easy carbohydrates for low blood sugar

Alcohol interferes with your liver's ability to release stored glucose into your blood. After a night of drinking, especially if you skipped dinner, your blood sugar can dip, which adds to the shakiness, fatigue, weakness, and fog that make a hangover miserable.

Sushi rice is white, short-grain rice seasoned with rice vinegar, a little sugar, and salt. It's about as easy a carbohydrate as you can eat. It digests quickly, it's bland, and it rarely bothers a sensitive stomach. That's the same reason people reach for toast, crackers, or plain pasta when they feel rough. A few pieces of sushi give you a steady, gentle dose of glucose without a heavy, greasy meal sitting in your gut.

### 2. The salt: replacing what you lost

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you pee more than you drink, and you lose sodium and other electrolytes along the way. Sweating and any vomiting add to the losses.

Sushi meals carry salt in several places: the seasoned rice, the soy sauce, the miso soup, the pickled vegetables, and the seaweed. A modest amount of salt, taken with fluid, helps your body actually hold on to the water you drink rather than passing it straight through. That's the same principle behind oral rehydration drinks. (More on the soy sauce trap below.)

### 3. The miso soup: warm fluid plus sodium

Miso soup may be the most useful thing on the table. It's mostly water, it's warm and easy to sip, and it contains sodium from the miso paste. A small bowl is a gentle way to start getting fluids and electrolytes in when plain water feels like too much. Warm, salty broth is a hangover staple across many cultures for a reason, and our guide to the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) covers the wider family.

### 4. The ginger: help for a queasy stomach

The thin pink slices of pickled ginger (gari) next to your sushi aren't just a palate cleanser. Ginger has decent evidence for easing nausea in some settings, such as morning sickness in pregnancy and nausea after surgery. There is no good evidence that it treats hangovers specifically, and the amount in a few slices of pickled ginger is small. Still, if nausea is your main complaint, nibbling a little ginger is harmless and may help.

### 5. The fish: protein that's easy to digest

Salmon, tuna, and other fish give you protein without much grease. Protein helps a meal keep you full and evens out the blood sugar spike from the rice. Oily fish like salmon also contains omega-3 fats, which are good for you in general, though there is no good evidence that one sushi lunch changes how bad your hangover feels.

## Is Raw Fish Okay When You're Hungover?

For most people, yes, if it comes from a place you trust. Raw fish served at a reputable sushi restaurant is handled to reduce the risk of parasites and bacteria, and a hangover doesn't make you more likely to get food poisoning.

The bigger issue is how your stomach feels. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and some people find raw, cold food unappealing or hard to keep down the morning after. If you're queasy, a few simple swaps make the meal gentler:

- **Choose cooked options.** Cooked shrimp (ebi), eel (unagi), crab or imitation crab, egg (tamago), and cooked salmon rolls are all easy to find.
- **Go vegetable-only.** Cucumber rolls (kappa maki), avocado rolls, and sweet potato rolls are mild and filling.
- **Be careful with grocery-store sushi.** Pre-packaged sushi can be fine, but check the date, keep it cold, and eat it soon after buying. Rice that sits out at room temperature for hours is a known food-safety risk.

Some people should avoid raw fish regardless of how they feel: people who are pregnant, people with weakened immune systems, and young children. That rule doesn't change after a night out.

## The Best Sushi Order for a Hangover

If you want a simple plan, here's how to build the meal, roughly in order of usefulness.

| What to order | Why it helps | Hangover tip |
|---|---|---|
| Miso soup | Warm fluid plus sodium | Start with this and sip it slowly |
| Simple rolls or nigiri | Easy carbs from the rice, light protein from fish | Salmon, tuna, cucumber, avocado, or cooked shrimp |
| Edamame | Protein, fiber, and potassium | Lightly salted is fine; you lost salt overnight |
| Pickled ginger | May ease mild nausea | Nibble between pieces |
| Seaweed salad | Minerals and a little fiber | Often sweet and salty; a small side is plenty |
| Water or green tea | Fluids, and a little caffeine from the tea | Drink a full glass of water with the meal |
| Tamago (sweet egg) | Gentle protein, cooked | Good if raw fish sounds bad today |

### What to skip or limit

- **Tempura rolls and fried toppings.** Fried food is heavy, slow to digest, and more likely to bother an irritated stomach. If you're craving it anyway, see our honest take on [greasy food for a hangover](/never-hungover/greasy-food-hangover).
- **Spicy mayo and creamy sauces.** Rich and fatty, and the spice can aggravate heartburn. Our guide to [spicy food and hangovers](/never-hungover/spicy-food-hangover) explains why some people feel worse after heat.
- **Lots of wasabi.** A little is fine. A big hit of wasabi on a sensitive stomach is a gamble.
- **Sake, beer, or a "hair of the dog" drink.** Another drink only postpones the hangover. It doesn't fix anything, and it adds more alcohol for your body to clear.
- **A mountain of soy sauce.** See the next section.

## The Soy Sauce Trap

Salt helps a hangover, but soy sauce is extremely concentrated. Regular soy sauce has close to 1,000 mg of sodium in a single tablespoon, which is a big chunk of the 2,300 mg daily limit recommended in US dietary guidelines. Dunking every piece of sushi in a full dish of it can push a single meal well past that.

Too much salt at once can make you feel thirstier and more bloated, and some people notice puffiness the next day. If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or kidney problems, or your doctor has told you to watch your salt, this matters even more.

A few easy habits keep it in check:

- Pour a small amount and refill rather than filling the dish.
- Dip the fish side lightly, not the rice side, which soaks it up like a sponge.
- Ask for low-sodium soy sauce. Most sushi places have it, and it typically has noticeably less sodium than regular.
- Let the miso soup and seasoned rice do some of the salt work.

## Sushi and Hydration: What Actually Matters Most

Food helps, but fluids matter more. A plate of sushi with no water is only a partial fix. The meal works best when you pair it with steady drinking over the next few hours.

A realistic plan for a hangover morning:

1. **Drink a glass of water before you eat**, or at least start sipping as soon as you sit down.
2. **Have the miso soup first.** It's the gentlest way to get fluid and salt into you.
3. **Eat slowly.** A few pieces, a pause, then a few more. Your stomach will tell you when to stop.
4. **Keep drinking water or unsweetened green tea** with and after the meal.
5. **Consider an electrolyte drink later** if you're still thirsty, headachy, or lightheaded. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers what works best.

About the green tea: it has some caffeine, usually less than coffee. If you normally drink coffee, a little caffeine can head off a withdrawal headache on top of the hangover. If you're already dehydrated or your heart feels jumpy, stick mostly to water.

## The Japanese Hangover Tradition: Shijimi Miso Soup

In Japan, one of the best-known hangover foods is miso soup made with shijimi, tiny freshwater clams. It's sold in convenience stores and instant packets, and many people swear by it after a night out.

Shijimi clams contain an amino acid called ornithine, and Japanese supplement makers market ornithine for "liver support" and next-day recovery. The honest picture: there is no good evidence from solid human trials that shijimi soup or ornithine relieves hangovers. What the soup does reliably deliver is the same thing any miso soup delivers: warm fluid, salt, and a little protein. If you see it on a menu, it's a good choice. Just don't expect a special effect beyond that.

Other traditional Japanese morning-after foods include umeboshi (salty pickled plums), often eaten with plain rice or rice porridge (okayu), and simple rice balls (onigiri). The common thread is the same: plain rice, salt, and something warm. Korea has its own hangover-soup tradition built on the same idea, which we cover in our guide to [Korean hangover soup](/never-hungover/korean-hangover-soup).

## Sushi vs. Other Hangover Foods

How does sushi stack up against the usual suspects? Here's a fair comparison.

| Food | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Sushi with miso soup | Easy carbs, salt, warm fluid, light protein, low grease | Soy sauce can push sodium very high; raw fish may not appeal |
| Eggs on toast | Protein, easy carbs, cooked and familiar | Easy to add a lot of butter or grease |
| Bananas | Potassium, easy carbs, no cooking | Not much else; light on salt and protein |
| Greasy breakfast or burger | Satisfying, calorie-dense | Heavy, slow to digest, can worsen nausea and heartburn |
| Pho or noodle soup | Lots of warm fluid and salt, easy carbs | High sodium broth; can be large |
| Plain crackers or toast | Very gentle on the stomach | Little protein or fluid |

Sushi lands in the good middle ground: more balanced than crackers, lighter than a fry-up. For the full list of what works and why, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover). If you're more in the mood for a classic, [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) breaks down why they're a staple.

## Eating Sushi Before Drinking

Sushi is also a decent meal to eat *before* a night out. Having food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol moves from your stomach into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That means a slower rise in blood alcohol and, for many people, a less punishing night.

A meal with some carbohydrate, protein, and a little fat tends to do this better than an empty stomach or a light snack. A few rolls with salmon or avocado, plus edamame and miso soup, fits that bill well. Our evidence-based guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) goes into more detail.

One caution: eating first doesn't make it safe to drink more. It slows absorption; it doesn't erase the alcohol. You'll still absorb most of it, just more gradually.

## Common Myths About Sushi and Hangovers

**"Seaweed detoxes your liver."** There is no good evidence for this. Seaweed contains minerals like iodine and some fiber, and it's a fine food, but your liver clears alcohol at its own pace. Nothing on a sushi menu speeds that up.

**"Wasabi clears the hangover out of your system."** Wasabi can make your eyes water and your sinuses feel clear for a moment. That's it. It doesn't affect how your body processes alcohol.

**"Raw fish is dangerous when you're hungover."** Not because of the hangover. Raw fish carries the same small risk it always does, which is why choosing a trustworthy place matters. If your stomach is upset, cooked options are simply more comfortable.

**"Sushi and sake is a good hangover combo."** Drinking more alcohol the next morning delays the hangover rather than treating it, and it adds to the load on your body. Save the sake for another day.

**"Any food will fix a hangover if you eat enough."** Food helps with low blood sugar and gives you energy, but it can't undo poor sleep or the inflammation that comes with heavy drinking. Time, fluids, and rest do most of the work.

## How Long Until You Feel Better?

Most hangovers fade within about 24 hours, and many people feel noticeably better a few hours after eating and rehydrating. A good meal doesn't shorten the timeline dramatically, but it often takes the edge off the worst of it, especially the weak, shaky, low-energy feeling that comes from low blood sugar.

If you're still feeling very unwell more than a day later, or your symptoms are getting worse instead of better, that's a sign something else might be going on. Go back to the warning box at the top of this page and check whether any of those signs apply.

## A Better Plan for Next Time

Sushi is a nice way to recover, but the most effective hangover strategy is still what you do the night before. The habits with the best evidence are simple: eat a real meal before you drink, pace yourself, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through each one.

Some people also add a supplement to their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. If you want to try it, take it alongside the habits above rather than instead of them. A well-reviewed, budget-friendly option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular higher-dose blend. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands side by side.

## The Bottom Line

- Sushi is a solid hangover meal: easy carbohydrates from the rice, salt and warm fluid from the miso soup, light protein from the fish, and ginger that may help mild nausea.
- Keep it simple. Miso soup, plain rolls or nigiri, edamame, pickled ginger, and lots of water.
- Go light on soy sauce. A tablespoon carries close to 1,000 mg of sodium, and low-sodium soy sauce is an easy swap.
- Choose cooked or vegetable rolls if your stomach is unsettled, and skip fried rolls, spicy mayo, and any morning-after sake.
- Food helps, but fluids and rest matter more. Sushi eases a hangover; it doesn't cure one.
- If you have warning signs like repeated vomiting, confusion, chest pain, or trouble breathing, get medical help instead of waiting it out.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is sushi good for a hangover?**

Yes, for most people sushi is a good hangover meal. The rice provides easy carbohydrates when your blood sugar may be low, miso soup adds warm fluid and sodium, and the fish gives you light protein without much grease. Pickled ginger may also help with mild nausea. It won't cure a hangover, but it's gentler and more balanced than a heavy, greasy breakfast.

**Is it safe to eat raw fish when you're hungover?**

For most healthy adults, yes, as long as it comes from a reputable restaurant or a fresh, properly refrigerated store package. A hangover doesn't raise your risk of food poisoning. If your stomach feels unsettled, cooked options like shrimp, eel, crab, cooked salmon, or egg rolls are easier to tolerate. People who are pregnant or have weakened immune systems should avoid raw fish regardless.

**Is miso soup good for a hangover?**

Miso soup is one of the better hangover foods. It's mostly water, it's warm and easy to sip, and it contains sodium, which helps your body hold on to fluids after alcohol has made you lose them. Start your meal with it and sip slowly. If you're watching your salt intake, one bowl is plenty.

**What is the best sushi to eat with a hangover?**

Keep it simple. Salmon or tuna nigiri, cucumber or avocado rolls, cooked shrimp, and tamago (sweet egg) are all good choices. Pair them with miso soup, edamame, pickled ginger, and plenty of water. Skip tempura rolls, rolls drowned in spicy mayo, and big amounts of wasabi if your stomach is sensitive.

**Is soy sauce bad for a hangover?**

A little is fine and can help replace lost salt. The problem is the amount: regular soy sauce has close to 1,000 mg of sodium per tablespoon, so heavy dipping can push one meal past a full day's recommended sodium. That can leave you thirstier and more bloated. Pour a small amount, dip the fish side lightly, or ask for low-sodium soy sauce.

**Does seaweed help a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that seaweed treats hangovers or detoxes your liver. It contains some minerals, including iodine, and a little fiber, so it's a fine part of the meal. Any benefit from a sushi meal comes mainly from the rice, the fluids, and the salt, not from the seaweed itself.

**Is it good to eat sushi before drinking?**

A sushi meal before drinking is a reasonable choice. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed, which means a gentler rise in blood alcohol. A mix of rice, fish or avocado, and edamame works better than a light snack. Eating first doesn't make it safe to drink more, though; it slows absorption rather than removing alcohol.

**Is shijimi clam miso soup a real hangover cure?**

Shijimi miso soup is a popular hangover food in Japan, and the clams contain an amino acid called ornithine that's often marketed for liver support. There is no good evidence from solid human trials that it relieves hangovers beyond what any warm, salty soup provides. It's still a good choice, because the fluid and sodium are genuinely helpful.
